codex.worst_flaw: The reward’s safety gate has a launch-blocking blind spot because the weekly audit samples only credited app checklists, leaving it unable to detect an increase in jobs started without any valid safety check.

claude.worst_flaw: Approved paper fallback checks stay in the denominator without earning credit, so a crew-level group reward can push technicians away from the safe fallback and toward peer pressure, and only five jobs per week are sampled for quality across all crews.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid setup, safety-quality guardrails, privacy and a randomized stagger make it approvable and fair, but the paid hour off for 70% adoption is a modest reward, the verification and counting rules are heavy, and durability rests on the fixed workflow more than on the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The pilot audits only credited digital jobs, so it cannot reliably detect whether reward pressure discourages approved paper fallback or leads technicians to skip required checks on uncredited jobs.

claude.worst_flaw: Operability and audit are thin: one coordinator checks counts against existing records, and the design has no replayable event or policy history, no independent shadow validation of the counting rule, and no staffed escalation path for appeals beyond that coordinator. It also sets one 65% crew threshold for every crew, not tied to each crew's baseline, and its follow-up after rewards end tracks only digital completion, not checklist quality.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a collective time-off reward, a clear counting rule with paper fallback, safeguards against rushing or gaming, and a staggered rollout that can measure its own effect make this a defensible pilot, but a one-hour reward over four weeks is modest, the process is heavy to administer, and the habit probably only lasts if the workflow fixes remove the friction.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no replayable event and policy versioning and no independent shadow validation, and the QA sample of five jobs a week is too thin to reliably catch rushed or backdated checklists before the group reward pays out.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot should not launch as written because using the approved paper fallback can cost the crew paid time, creating pressure to bypass it when safety or access requires it.

holistic.reason: Union-aware, group-level reward with a fair counting rule, safety guardrails, pause triggers and a randomized stepped rollout is approvable, though a one-hour reward is small, group-level pay-off dilutes individual line of sight, and lasting change rests mainly on the app-default fix.

claude.worst_flaw: The 80% group target has no basis in the measured baseline, and the 'baseline' in the decision rule is taken during weeks 1–2, while the queue fixes are already running. Only a two-week comparison window with shared reviewers then separates the reward from the workflow changes, and nothing handles PR size or complexity.

codex.worst_flaw: With one group per condition and reviewers working across both groups, the pilot cannot reliably distinguish the reward’s effect from differences in PR mix, reviewer coverage, or spillover.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real queue bottleneck first, uses a modest team-wide reward, and has clear definitions and safeguards against gaming, but a one-hour reward is small and the pilot is complex enough that awareness and durability past the reward window are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot reliably isolate the reward’s effect because the single-queue comparison uses an earlier period and the staggered rollout leaves differences in PR volume, complexity and timing unaccounted for.

claude.worst_flaw: The evaluation compares a short fixes-only period, or two staggered groups, with fixed 80% thresholds and no handling of uncertainty, seasonality or spillover between groups, and it does not check review quality after the reward ends; the keep/change/drop decision could rest on noise.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck (protected review time, routing, backup), uses a clear measurable rule with anti-gaming checks and no individual scoring, and removes the reward with a keep/change/drop test, but the 8-hour clock is stricter than the one-day goal and the team-level reward plus 45 minutes a week of owner overhead may leave sceptical engineers unmoved, so the lasting effect depends on the workflow fixes sticking.

claude.worst_flaw: A group-wide all-or-nothing 80% threshold, which also equals the final keep target, rewards the whole group or none of it and invites rubber-stamp first reviews. Only a weekly sample of five reviews guards against that, and there is no baseline check that 80% is achievable from a 2.6-day median or any measure of author-side quality such as rework or defects.

codex.worst_flaw: The paid afternoon hinges on an 80% threshold with no demonstrated feasibility, no rule for groups with few or zero eligible PRs, and no adjustment for review complexity.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real bottleneck (queue, routing, coverage) before adding a modest, group-level, anti-gaming-guarded reward with a clear exit plan, though the measurement rules are heavy and a one-afternoon prize may feel small to sceptical engineers.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk rollout decision uses an invalid measure of logging adoption: one entry per shift can clear the 90% threshold even if most eligible moments go unlogged.

claude.worst_flaw: The exit decision depends on kiosk coverage by shift, where a single entry marks a shift as covered. That measure is easy to game and says little about how many hand-hygiene moments are actually logged, so the persistence rule rests on a weak proxy.

holistic.reason: Rewards independently audited behaviour with fair baselines, sensible safeguards and a staggered design, but a team meal is a modest incentive and the monthly audit is a slow, noisy feedback loop, so it is complex and offers little to keep the habit once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk adoption measure is a launch blocker because it excludes actions whose logging observers cannot see, so differences in kiosk visibility or delayed entry can drive keep-or-drop decisions even when actual adoption is unchanged.

claude.worst_flaw: The ward-level kiosk logging share depends on observers seeing whether each action was logged, which they often can't, so the main adoption measure risks being too small and biased to support the keep, revise or drop decision. There is also no event history, no shadow check against the kiosk logs, and no appeals process.

holistic.reason: It rewards audited hand hygiene rather than kiosk logging, uses safe guardrails and a clear stop rule, and fixes the kiosk friction first, but a team meal is a modest, delayed reward and the effect on logging after the reward ends is uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The design rewards ward-level compliance from monthly observer audits, which observers can easily influence (the Hawthorne effect) and which draw on small samples, and the kiosk logging the hospital actually asked for is given no defined role or validated purpose beyond spotting workflow problems, so neither the measurement nor the comparison across a staggered rollout of three wards can reliably show an effect.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot can meet its reward and persistence targets without measuring what share of eligible hand-hygiene moments nurses actually log.

holistic.reason: The proposal is carefully designed, with a ward-level reward tied to audited compliance rather than kiosk entries, a staggered rollout, and an explicit decision rule, but a catered meal is a weak incentive, nurses may barely notice it, and the behaviour is likely to fade once the reward is removed.

codex.worst_flaw: The fixed 60% reward threshold treats every resolved ticket as an eligible opportunity without verifying how often agents in each queue can safely link or create a useful article.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never tests or reconciles the conflict with the existing CSAT bonus, so agents may lose bonus pay by spending time writing articles. Its causal test is also weak: only weeks 4 and 5 compare a few team clusters, and the week 6 workflow change confounds wave two's results.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with clean counting rules, QA and CSAT guardrails, a staggered test, and workflow fixes that persist, but the 45-minute break reward is modest, the 60% jump from 12% is steep, and the proposal is dense and administratively complex for agents to grasp.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-week comparison sets no minimum worthwhile reward effect and gives no plan to quantify uncertainty across teams, leaving the value of paid time off unresolved.

claude.worst_flaw: The weeks 3-4 within-group comparison cannot isolate what the reward adds: both groups get the same fixes and feedback, one group is already earning rewards in that window, and the workflow change made mid-window confounds the result. With only two group-level clusters, the stop rule at 20% and 35% rests on weak evidence.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with fixes before rewards, randomized stepped rollout, QA sampling, and CSAT guardrails, but the 1-hour time-off reward is modest, the 40% group threshold is a big jump from 12%, and without ongoing rewards the habit may fade even with the improved workflow.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until an independent check can detect whether agents discourage legitimate ticket reopenings to protect their team's paid time off.

claude.worst_flaw: The design uses a team-level all-or-nothing PTO milestone with only light QA sampling (10 tickets per week across 60 agents) and no check of how CSAT bonus pressure interacts with the extra article work. That leaves room for generic or irrelevant links and for free-riding inside a team. The stagger also runs only 3 randomized waves of teams, and the workflow change in week 6 contaminates the comparison.

holistic.reason: Fixes workflow friction first, counts credit only for QA-checked, stay-closed tickets, protects CSAT and reopen rates, and staggers rollout so it can be measured; the team-level time-off reward is modest and may fade once it ends, though the default link field should help habits stick.
